output.title: When glossary upkeep stops being a useful manual task
output.body:
If glossary upkeep is starting to feel like a small tax on every week, the first question is not “Can AI do it?” It is “Is this the same decision repeated often enough to deserve a workflow?” For a small business, glossary work only becomes a bounded automation candidate when it is recurring, uses clear rules, and pulls you away from customer work or sales. If every term needs a fresh judgment, or the source material is patchy, automation can become a tidy way to create confusion. Efficient confusion is still confusion.

The practical next step is simple: write down one week of glossary changes and mark each item with three labels — source, decision rule, and approval owner. Source means where the term came from: FAQ, CRM note, product copy, internal doc. Decision rule means the plain-English rule you used: brand voice, definition match, delete, merge, or flag for review. Approval owner means who can publish it. If the list is short and ad hoc, keep it manual. If the same rule keeps appearing, you may have a bounded pilot.

That pilot should stay narrow: propose changes, batch them, and keep human sign-off before publication. Bareni works as a consulting practice being built, so the point here is not a grand promise; it is to separate repeatable glossary maintenance from one-off judgment before you spend money or time on the wrong fix.
